title: Deadlock: four conditions and how to break one
objective: By the end of this lesson you can recognise a deadlock from a running process, name the four conditions that must all hold, and remove the one that is practical to remove.

blocks.text: A deadlock is a set of threads each waiting for something another of them holds. Nothing is broken, nothing crashes, no error is reported — the threads simply wait, correctly, forever. It is the quietest failure in this course, and once you know its signature it is also one of the fastest to diagnose.

blocks.caption: Two mutexes, two orders
lines: lock(B);   <- waits for T2         lock(A);   <- waits for T1
/* Each holds what the other needs to continue. Neither will let go,
because letting go is what happens after acquiring the second lock. */

blocks.text: Verified: with this inconsistent order, the program hangs. With both threads taking A then B, it completes immediately, every time. The code inside the critical sections was identical — only the order changed.

rows: Only one thread can hold the resource
Rarely — it is usually the point
A thread holds one resource while requesting another
Sometimes: take everything at once, or nothing
A resource cannot be taken away from its holder
Sometimes: use trylock and back off
A cycle of threads each waiting on the next
Yes — and this is the practical answer

blocks.title: In practice you break circular wait, with an ordering rule
blocks.text: Define a global order over your locks and require every thread to acquire them in that order. If everyone takes A before B, no cycle can form — the thread holding B has already passed A, so it is not waiting for it. The rule is easy to state, easy to review, and costs nothing at runtime. Write the order down beside the lock declarations; an ordering that lives only in the author's memory is not an ordering.
Recognising one at three in the morning

items: The process is alive but produces nothing new
CPU usage is zero — verified above: the deadlocked process showed 0.0%
It responds to SIGKILL but not to anything requiring its own progress
No error, no log entry, no crash

blocks.caption: The diagnosis, which takes about thirty seconds
lines: 4394 Sl    0.0 d              <- alive, sleeping, using nothing
# The cycle is right there: t2 wants A, t1 wants B, and each holds the other.

blocks.title: The backtrace names the variable, not just the address
blocks.text: In the real output above, gdb printed <A> and <B> beside the futex addresses because the program was built with -g. Building your production binaries with debug symbols — even when you ship them stripped and keep the symbols separately — is what turns a three-hour incident into a three-minute one.
The other ways to get there

items: Locking the same non-recursive mutex twice in one thread — a deadlock with a single thread and a single lock
Taking a lock inside a callback that the lock holder invokes
Two subsystems that each take their own lock and then call into the other
A lock held while waiting on a condition variable that only another holder of that lock can signal

blocks.caption: Try, and back off
lines: if (pthread_mutex_trylock(&B) != 0) {   /* would block? then do not */
/* wait a moment and start over — the cycle cannot form */
/* This trades a guarantee for a retry loop. Prefer an ordering rule;
use this when the set of locks is not known until run time. */

blocks.title: Deadlock a program, then diagnose it as if you had not written it
steps: Write two threads: one locks A then B, the other locks B then A, with a short sleep between the two locks
Run it — it should hang within a second
From another terminal: ps -o pid,stat,%cpu -p <pid>     and confirm CPU is 0.0
Run: gdb -p <pid> -batch -ex 'thread apply all bt'      (build with -g first)
Find the two futex_wait frames and name which lock each thread is waiting for
Fix it by making both threads take A then B — confirm it now completes every run
Break it a different way: have one thread lock A twice in a row, and diagnose that too
Optional: rewrite the fix using trylock and back-off, and explain what you gave up
blocks.expected: A hang with zero CPU, a backtrace showing the cycle, and a one-line ordering change that removes it permanently. The single-thread double-lock is worth doing as well: it teaches that a deadlock needs neither two threads nor two locks — just a wait that nothing can end.

cheatsheet: Deadlock = threads each waiting for what another holds; correct code, no progress
Signature: alive, zero CPU, no error, no log
Four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait
In practice, break circular wait: define a global lock order and always follow it
Write the lock order beside the declarations
Diagnose with: ps (zero CPU) then gdb -p <pid> -batch -ex 'thread apply all bt'
Build with -g so the backtrace names the locks, not just addresses
Locking a non-recursive mutex twice in one thread deadlocks that thread alone
trylock plus back-off works when the lock set is only known at run time

checkpoint.prompt: Which of the four conditions is the one usually removed in practice?

choices.B: Hold and wait for a second resource
choices.C: Mutual exclusion of the shared data

checkpoint.explanation: Mutual exclusion is usually the whole reason the lock exists. Removing circular wait — by defining and following a global lock order — is free at run time and easy to review, which is why it is the standard answer.

checkpoint.prompt: A service stops responding. It is alive, has no errors, and uses 0% CPU. What do you run first?

choices.A: strace to see which system calls it makes
choices.B: Check the free disk space first
choices.D: Restart it and see if it recovers

checkpoint.explanation: Zero CPU means nothing is executing, so a syscall trace shows nothing new. The backtrace shows where every thread is waiting — and the cycle is usually visible immediately.

checkpoint.prompt: Can a single thread deadlock itself with a single mutex?

choices.A: No — deadlock requires at least two threads
choices.B: Only on a single-core machine without preemption
choices.C: Only with recursive mutexes held twice
choices.D: Yes — relocking a mutex it already holds

checkpoint.explanation: Locking a non-recursive mutex the thread already holds makes it wait for itself. The general condition is a wait that nothing can end. Two threads and two locks is the common shape, not a requirement.

checkpoint.prompt: What does trylock-and-back-off give up compared with a lock ordering rule?

choices.B: A guarantee — it turns into retries
choices.C: Thread safety of the surrounding code
choices.D: The ability to use condition variables

checkpoint.explanation: Ordering makes the cycle structurally impossible; back-off replaces that with a retry loop that can repeat, at the cost of retries and, in the worst case, threads that keep retrying against each other.
